kcet|Physics|2009|3|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times (Kepler's second law), so it moves
**fastest where it is closest to the Sun**.
**Step 1 — locate the Sun.** The figure puts the Sun at the **left focus** of the ellipse,
not at the centre ✓ That is Kepler's first law: the Sun occupies one focus.
**Step 2 — find the nearest point.** Of the four marked points, **A** is the left-hand end
of the major axis — the end **on the Sun's side**. It is therefore the **perihelion**, the
closest approach ✓ (C, the opposite end, is the aphelion and the farthest.)
**Step 3 — apply Kepler's second law.** The line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal
areas in equal times. Near the Sun that line is **short**, so the planet must travel a
**long** arc to sweep the same area — it moves fastest ✓ Far from the Sun the line is
long, so a short arc suffices and the planet crawls.
So the speed is greatest at **A** ✓
**The same conclusion from angular momentum.** No torque acts about the Sun, since gravity
is central, so
**L = m v r = constant**
Hence **v ∝ 1/r** at the two ends of the major axis, where v is perpendicular to r ✓ The
smallest r gives the largest v, and the smallest r is at **A**.
**A check with the energy.** Total energy is conserved:
½mv² − GMm/r = constant
At small r the potential term −GMm/r is **more negative**, so the kinetic term must be
**larger** to compensate ✓ again giving maximum speed at perihelion.
**Reading the distractors.**
**C** ✗ is the **aphelion**, the farthest point — where the planet is **slowest**. It is
the exact opposite of the answer, and the commonest wrong choice if the Sun's focus is
misread as the right-hand one.
**B** and **D** ✗ are the ends of the **minor** axis. There the planet's distance from the
Sun equals the semi-major axis, so its speed is intermediate — neither maximum nor
minimum ✓
**The numbers for the Earth.** At perihelion (147 million km) the Earth moves at about
**30·3 km/s**; at aphelion (152 million km) about **29·3 km/s** ✓ a small difference,
because the orbit is nearly circular, but in the direction the law predicts.
∴ A.
kcet|Physics|2017|6|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
The **equipartition theorem** gives ½kT of energy to each degree of freedom, and a
monatomic ideal gas molecule has three.
**Step 1 — count the degrees of freedom.** An ideal gas molecule is treated as a point
mass that can move in three independent directions:
**x, y and z** — that is **3** translational degrees of freedom ✓
**Step 2 — apply equipartition.** Each degree of freedom carries a mean energy of
**½kT**
so the mean total energy per molecule is
3 × ½kT = **(3/2)kT** ✓
**Where the ½kT comes from.** For motion along x, the mean kinetic energy is
⟨½mvₓ²⟩ = **½kT**
and the same for y and z. Adding the three gives ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)kT ✓
**A check through the gas laws.** One mole contains N_A molecules, so the internal energy
of a mole of monatomic gas is
U = N_A × (3/2)kT = **(3/2)RT**
since R = N_A k ✓ — the standard result, and it confirms the per-molecule value.
**A check through pressure.** Kinetic theory gives PV = (1/3)Nm⟨v²⟩, and combining with
PV = NkT:
(1/3)m⟨v²⟩ = kT
so ½m⟨v²⟩ = **(3/2)kT** ✓ the mean kinetic energy per molecule, by a third route.
**Reading the distractors.**
**½kT** ✗ is the energy of **one** degree of freedom, not all three — the commonest error.
**kT** ✗ would correspond to two degrees of freedom, as in a two-dimensional gas.
**2kT** ✗ would need four.
Counting **three** translational directions is the whole question ✓
**A caution about diatomic gases.** A diatomic molecule adds two **rotational** degrees of
freedom, giving (5/2)kT at ordinary temperatures, and vibrational modes add more at high
temperature. The phrase "ideal gas" in this question means the simple monatomic model,
where only translation counts ✓
∴ (3/2)kT.
kcet|Physics|2014|17|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
In a **banked turn** the horizontal component of the lift supplies the centripetal force
while the vertical component carries the weight — and their ratio gives the familiar
tan θ relation.
**Step 1 — convert the speed to SI units.**
720 km/h = 720 × 1000/3600 = **200 m s⁻¹**
**Step 2 — state the banking relation.** Resolving the lift L at angle θ to the vertical:
vertical: L cos θ = **mg**
horizontal: L sin θ = **mv²/r**
Dividing the second by the first:
**tan θ = v²/(rg)**
**Step 3 — rearrange for the radius.**
r = v²/(g tan θ)
**Step 4 — substitute**, with θ = 45° so tan θ = **1**, and g = 10 m s⁻²:
r = (200)²/(10 × 1)
= 40000/10
= 4000 m
= **4 km** ✓
**Why the mass does not appear.** It cancels when the two equations are divided ✓ so the
radius of the loop is the same for a light aircraft and a heavy one at the same speed and
bank angle.
**Why 45° is convenient.** At that angle tan θ = 1, so the relation reduces to
**r = v²/g** ✓ — the turn radius equals the speed squared over gravity, with no
trigonometry to evaluate.
**A check on the magnitude.** A 4 km radius for a 200 m/s aircraft is realistic: the
centripetal acceleration is v²/r = 40000/4000 = **10 m s⁻²**, exactly 1g sideways ✓ which
is what a 45° bank must produce, since the horizontal and vertical components of lift are
then equal.
**Reading the distractors.**
**7·2 km** ✗ comes from using 720 without converting from km/h — dividing 720² by 10 and
then mis-scaling.
**2 km** ✗ is half the answer, as if tan 45° had been taken as 2.
**4·5 km** ✗ is close but corresponds to g = 8·9.
The conversion 720 km/h = **200 m/s** is the step most often dropped, and it is worth
doing first ✓
∴ 4 km.
kcet|Physics|2018|21|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
The block **rests** on the plane, so it is in equilibrium and the friction exactly
balances the pull of gravity along the slope. The coefficient 0·8 is not needed.
**Step 1 — resolve the weight along the incline.** For a plane at θ = 30°, the component
of the weight down the slope is
**mg sin θ**
**Step 2 — impose equilibrium.** The block is at rest, so the friction force balances it:
f = mg sin θ
**10 = m × 10 × sin 30°**
**Step 3 — solve.**
10 = m × 10 × 0·5
10 = 5m
**m = 2 kg** ✓
**Why the coefficient of friction is a red herring.** μ gives the **maximum** friction
available, not the friction actually acting. A static block uses only as much as it needs:
maximum available = μ mg cos 30° = 0·8 × 2 × 10 × 0·866 = **13·86 N**
actual friction = **10 N** ✓
Since 10 < 13·86, the block can indeed rest ✓ and the problem is consistent. Using
f = μmg cos θ instead would give m = 10/(0·8 × 10 × 0·866) = **1·44 kg**, which is not
offered — a sign that the static reading is intended.
**The distinction being tested.** **Static** friction adjusts itself to whatever is needed,
up to μ_s N. **Kinetic** friction is fixed at μ_k N. Here the block is stationary, so the
first applies and the stated 10 N **is** the friction ✓
**Check the numbers.** With m = 2 kg:
weight = **20 N**
component along the slope = 20 sin 30° = **10 N** ✓ matching the given friction exactly.
component perpendicular = 20 cos 30° = **17·3 N**, so the normal force is 17·3 N and the
maximum friction is 0·8 × 17·3 = 13·86 N ✓ comfortably more than required.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 kg** would need only 5 N of friction, **3 kg** would need
15 N (more than the 13·86 N available, so it could not rest) and **4 kg** would need 20 N
✗ Only 2 kg makes mg sin 30° equal to exactly 10 N ✓
∴ 2 kg.

kcet|Physics|2007|3|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch.s:
Water climbs the narrow channels of a plant fibre by **capillarity** — the rise of a
liquid in a fine tube against gravity.
**The mechanism.** Water **wets** cellulose, so its contact angle with the fibre wall is
small. Surface tension then pulls the liquid surface up the wall, and the curved meniscus
that forms has a lower pressure beneath it than the atmosphere outside. That pressure
difference drives the column upward until the weight of the raised water balances it:
**h = 2T cos θ/(ρ g r)**
with T the surface tension, θ the contact angle, ρ the density and **r the radius of the
channel** ✓
**Why plant fibres are so effective.** The height rises as **1/r**, so the finer the
channel the higher the water climbs ✓ Plant xylem vessels and fibres are only tens of
micrometres across, which is precisely why they lift water so far.
**A worked estimate.** For water, T ≈ 0·073 N m⁻¹, ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9·8 m s⁻², and
taking cos θ ≈ 1 for good wetting, a channel of radius 20 μm gives
h = 2(0·073)/(1000 × 9·8 × 20 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ **0·74 m**
— a substantial climb from surface tension alone ✓
**Why not viscosity.** Viscosity is the fluid's internal **friction**, which resists flow
rather than causing it ✗ A more viscous liquid rises **more slowly** up a capillary, but
to exactly the **same final height** — viscosity does not appear in the formula for h at
all ✓ It governs the rate, never the result.
**Why not fluid pressure.** Ordinary hydrostatic pressure acts **downward** through a
column and would, if anything, oppose the rise ✗ The relevant pressure here is the
**pressure drop across the curved meniscus**, which is a surface-tension effect — that is,
capillarity by another name.
**Why not osmosis.** Osmosis is the movement of solvent across a **semi-permeable
membrane** driven by a difference in solute concentration ✗ It does contribute to water
uptake by living roots, but a **fibre** is not a membrane, and the question asks about the
rise within the fibre itself ✓
∴ capillarity.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, viscosity. Viscosity resists flow and does
not enter the capillary-rise formula h = 2T cos θ/(ρgr) at all; the rise is caused by
surface tension in a narrow channel, which is capillarity. The key has been corrected to
the first option.

kcet|Physics|2009|6|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
Equal **apparent** weights in water means the heavier piece in air must be losing more to
buoyancy — and buoyancy depends on **volume**.
**Step 1 — write the apparent weights.** For a body of weight W and volume V fully
immersed,
apparent weight = W − ρ_w V g
Setting the two equal:
W_s − ρ_w V_s g = W_a − ρ_w V_a g
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
W_s − W_a = ρ_w g (V_s − V_a)
**Step 3 — bring in the densities.** Since V = W/(ρg):
W_s − W_a = ρ_w (W_s/ρ_s − W_a/ρ_a)
W_s(1 − ρ_w/ρ_s) = W_a(1 − ρ_w/ρ_a)
**W_s/W_a = (1 − ρ_w/ρ_a)/(1 − ρ_w/ρ_s)**
**Step 4 — substitute the densities**, with steel ≈ 7800, aluminium ≈ 2700 and water 1000
kg m⁻³:
numerator: 1 − 1000/2700 = **0·630**
denominator: 1 − 1000/7800 = **0·872**
W_s/W_a = 0·630/0·872 = **0·72**
so **W_s < W_a** — the **aluminium piece weighs more in air** ✓
**The reasoning without numbers.** Aluminium is **less dense**, so for a given weight it
occupies a **larger volume** and displaces more water. It therefore loses **more** weight
on immersion ✓ For the two to end up equal in water, the aluminium must have started
**heavier** in air.
**A concrete illustration.** Take the aluminium piece to weigh **100 N** in air. Its
volume is 100/(2700 × 9·8) = 3·78 × 10⁻³ m³, so it loses
1000 × 9·8 × 3·78 × 10⁻³ = **37·0 N** — an apparent weight of **63·0 N**.
For the steel piece to show the same 63·0 N, its air weight W satisfies
W(1 − 1000/7800) = 63·0, giving W = 63·0/0·872 = **72·2 N** ✓ lighter than the
aluminium's 100 N, as predicted.
**Reading the distractors.**
**"steel piece will weigh more"** ✗ is the intuitive answer — steel is the denser
material — but density is not weight. The question fixes the **immersed** weights, not
the volumes, and that reverses the comparison ✓
**"they have the same weight"** ✗ would require equal buoyant losses, hence equal volumes
— impossible for equal immersed weights at different densities.
**"half the weight"** ✗ the ratio is 0·72, not 0·5.
∴ aluminium piece will weigh more.
kcet|Physics|2011|10|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Terminal velocity varies as the **square of the radius**, so the key step is finding how
much the radius grows when eight drops merge.
**Step 1 — recall the terminal velocity.** Balancing weight, buoyancy and Stokes drag
gives
**v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η)**
so for given liquids, **v ∝ r²** ✓
**Step 2 — find the new radius.** Volume is conserved when the drops merge:
8 × (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)πR³
8r³ = R³
**R = 2r**
**Step 3 — scale the velocity.**
V/v = (R/r)² = 2² = **4**
so
V = 4 × 10 = **40 cm s⁻¹** ✓
**Why the radius only doubles.** Eight times the **volume** means only ∛8 = **2** times
the radius ✓ Volume grows as the cube, so a large increase in volume makes a modest
increase in size — and that is what keeps the answer at 40 rather than 80.
**The general rule.** Merging n equal drops gives R = n^(1/3) r, so
**V = n^(2/3) v**
With n = 8: V = 8^(2/3) v = **4v** ✓ The exponent 2/3 is the signature of this family of
problems.
**Why the big drop falls faster.** Weight grows as r³ while the drag grows only as r
(Stokes' law, F = 6πηrv), so the balance tips towards gravity as the drop enlarges ✓ A
bigger drop must fall faster before the drag catches up — which is why drizzle falls
gently and large raindrops come down hard.
**Reading the distractors.**
**80 cm s⁻¹** ✗ is 8v — the answer if the velocity were taken to scale with the
**volume** rather than with r². It is the commonest error here.
**10 cm s⁻¹** ✗ would mean merging changes nothing.
**30 cm s⁻¹** ✗ corresponds to no natural power.
A quick check: the answer must be **more** than 10 (bigger drops fall faster) but less
than 80 (the velocity grows more slowly than the volume) ✓ which leaves 40 and 30, and
the factor n^(2/3) = 4 settles it.
∴ 40 cm s⁻¹.
kcet|Physics|2011|11|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
The capillary rise is governed by
**h = 2T cos θ/(ρ g r)**
so **h ∝ 1/r** — the narrower the tube, the higher the water climbs.
**Step 1 — identify what varies.** Both tubes hold the **same liquid** (water) in the same
gravity, so T, θ, ρ and g are identical. Only the radius **r** differs ✓
**Step 2 — compare.** Since h is inversely proportional to r,
**smaller r ⟹ greater h**
so the rise is **greater in the tube of smaller diameter** ✓
**Why narrower means higher.** Two competing quantities scale differently with r:
the **upward pull** of surface tension acts along the circle of contact, of length 2πr —
so it grows as **r**
the **weight** of the raised column is ρg(πr²h) — so it grows as **r²h**
Balancing them, 2πrT cos θ = ρgπr²h, gives h ∝ **1/r** ✓ The perimeter that does the
lifting shrinks more slowly than the cross-section that must be lifted.
**A worked comparison.** For water with T = 0·073 N m⁻¹ and cos θ ≈ 1:
a tube of radius **0·5 mm** gives h = 2(0·073)/(1000 × 9·8 × 5 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ **30 mm**
a tube of radius **0·1 mm** gives h ≈ **149 mm** — five times as high for one fifth the
radius ✓ exactly the inverse proportionality.
**Reading the distractors.**
**"the same in both tubes"** ✗ would require h to be independent of r, but r sits in the
denominator ✓
**"greater in the tube of larger diameter"** ✗ reverses the proportionality — the trap for
anyone who reasons that a wider tube holds more water. It does, but it also has far more
weight to lift per unit of contact perimeter ✓
**"independent of the diameter"** ✗ is the same error as the first.
**A caution.** The formula assumes the tube is narrow enough for the meniscus to be
spherical, and that the tube is **long enough**. In a short tube the water rises to the
top and the meniscus simply flattens — it does not overflow ✓ a detail worth knowing,
though it does not affect the comparison here.
∴ greater in the tube of smaller diameter.
kcet|Physics|2017|16|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
A hydraulic lift multiplies force by transmitting pressure through a confined liquid —
that is **Pascal's law**.
**The law.** Pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted
**undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container** ✓
**How the lift uses it.** A small force F₁ on a piston of small area A₁ creates a pressure
P = F₁/A₁
That same pressure acts on the large piston of area A₂, producing
**F₂ = P A₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁)** ✓
Since A₂ ≫ A₁, the output force is many times the input — which is why a car can be
raised by hand.
**A worked example.** With A₁ = 10 cm² and A₂ = 1000 cm², a force of 200 N gives
F₂ = 200 × (1000/10) = **20000 N** — enough to lift two tonnes ✓
**Why energy is not created.** The large piston moves **less** far in the same proportion.
The liquid is incompressible, so the volumes swept are equal:
A₁d₁ = A₂d₂
and the work done is the same at both ends: F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ ✓ The lift trades distance for
force, exactly as a lever does.
**Why not the other laws.**
**Stoke's law** ✗ gives the viscous drag F = 6πηrv on a small sphere moving through a
fluid — relevant to falling drops, not to pressure transmission.
**Bernoulli's law** ✗ relates pressure, speed and height along a **streamline** in a
**moving** fluid. The liquid in a hydraulic lift is essentially static, and Bernoulli
explains aerofoils and venturi meters instead.
**Torricelli's law** ✗ gives the efflux speed v = √(2gh) of liquid escaping through a
hole — again a flow result, not a transmission one.
**The distinguishing feature.** A hydraulic lift involves a **confined, stationary**
liquid in which pressure is passed from one piston to another ✓ Static plus enclosed
points to Pascal; anything involving **motion** of the fluid points to Bernoulli or
Torricelli.
**Other applications of the same law.** Hydraulic brakes, the hydraulic press, and the
dentist's chair all work on Pascal's law ✓
∴ Pascal's law.
